# Lower speed limits and injury crashes in Victoria, 2023–2025: what the open data shows

<!-- Generated by `make report` from docs/templates/BRIEF.md.tmpl; every number comes from outputs/metrics.json. -->

**Briefing note** · Independent analysis of public Victorian Government data · Not a DTP product

## Bottom line

- Roads whose speed limit was lowered between mid-2023 and the end of 2024 had about **19% fewer
  injury crashes** afterwards than the trend on similar unchanged roads would predict. The plausible range is
  between 1% and 34% fewer.
- The result is **encouraging but not conclusive**. It rests on 191 injury crashes after the change, and
  3 of 8 reasonable variations of the analysis leave "no change" inside the plausible range.
- The **Fitzroy and Collingwood 30 km/h trial** points the same way: about 28% fewer injury crashes
  than expected. Its plausible range (anywhere from 50% fewer to 2% more) still includes "no change", because the trial area is too
  small to be sure. A study of this size would miss a real 20% reduction 73% of the time.

## What we looked at

DTP publishes a monthly map of every posted speed limit in Victoria. Comparing the maps over time shows
exactly which stretches of road had their limit lowered and roughly when. We found **1,109 road
segments (777 km, 206 separate speed-zone changes)** lowered between September 2023
and December 2024. We compared them with **271,949 segments whose limit never changed**,
matched on the original limit, the type of road and the council area.

For each segment we counted police-reported injury crashes in the three years before the change and in
the 12–27 months after it, up to December 2025, the latest complete month.

## What we found

| Roads where the limit was lowered | Injury crashes compared with expected |
|---|---|
| **All lowered roads** | **19% fewer** (between 1% and 34% fewer) |
| Fatal and serious-injury crashes only | 20% fewer (anywhere from 42% fewer to 10% more) |
| From 60 km/h to 40 or 50 km/h | 33% fewer (anywhere from 56% fewer to 2% more) |
| From 90–110 km/h to lower | 36% fewer (anywhere from 61% fewer to 5% more) |
| From 70 or 80 km/h to lower | 13% fewer (anywhere from 39% fewer to 24% more) |
| Local streets from 50 to 40 km/h | 3% fewer (anywhere from 31% fewer to 36% more) |

Read the ranges as "what the data cannot rule out". The overall result just excludes "no change". Each
road type on its own has too few crashes to say much yet. For high-speed roads, crashes on the treated
roads were already falling relative to comparison roads before the change (the fake-date test below gives
19% fewer for them), so part of that reduction may have been under way anyway. Local streets lowered to 40 km/h show no clear
change in the first year or two; quiet streets have few crashes to begin with, so they need longer follow-up.

## Why simple before-and-after counts mislead

Crash numbers move for many reasons besides speed limits: traffic returning after the 2020–21 lockdowns,
weather, enforcement, chance. To show why the comparison roads matter, we pretended the limits changed
three years earlier, when nothing actually happened:

- A simple before-and-after count on these roads would have reported crashes **up 13%**.
- The comparison roads rose by a similar amount (up 15%), so our method correctly reported **no
  change** (a 0% difference).
- A standard statistical correction for "roads picked because of a bad year" (Empirical Bayes) wrongly
  reported crashes **up 18%**. It depends on knowing how much traffic each road carries, and the public
  traffic counts stop in 2019. We therefore do not rely on it.

## How confident are we?

**Supports the result**
- The fake-date test above passes.
- The answer barely moves whether we use one year or five years of "before" data (between 20% and
  22% fewer). If the roads had been chosen because of a recent spike in crashes, it would move.
- 8 variations (how crashes are matched to roads, how change dates are handled, how roads are grouped)
  all point the same way, giving between 14% and 30% fewer.

**Limits it**
- Lower limits often come with other changes, such as new signs, traffic calming or roadworks. The data does
  not record these, so the result applies to the whole package, not the number on the sign alone.
- The date of each change is known only to within a few months.
- Current traffic volumes are not public. If traffic on the treated roads fell for other reasons, part of
  the drop would not be due to the change.
- This is observational data. It shows an association after accounting for trends on similar roads; it
  does not prove cause.

## Suggestions

1. **Record the date the signs went up, and any other works**, against each speed-zone change request. The
   request number is already in the public data. Accurate dates alone would sharpen every future evaluation.
2. **Record trial limits in the Speed Zones data.** The Fitzroy and Collingwood 30 km/h trial is missing from
   it, although police crash reports show the new limit (40% of crashes on trial streets were recorded
   as 30 km/h, up from 2%).
3. **Add operating speeds and current traffic volumes**, for example from connected-vehicle data. That would
   show whether speeds actually fell, and would fix the main weakness found here.
4. **Repeat the analysis as 2026 crash data arrives.** The pipeline reruns with one command; local-street
   changes in particular need more time.
5. **Republish the January 2024 Speed Zones file**, which downloads corrupted from the open data portal.

## About this analysis

Public data only (CC BY 4.0): Victoria road crash data, Speed Zones, historical traffic volumes and Vicmap
boundaries, all Victorian Government. The method is a comparison-group before-and-after design with
statistical checks; the full method, code and every table are in the project README. Analysis by Zhenqian
Liu. The views are the author's own.
